common_name: Magnum Bonum Apple (North Carolina Piedmont Heirloom Fall Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Magnum Bonum was raised from a Hall apple seed near Davidson College, North Carolina, around 1828 and has a moderate chill requirement of roughly 500-650 hours that let it thrive from the Piedmont into the Deep South, so plant another apple cultivar nearby since it is not reliably self-fruitful.

directions: Old Southern nurseries once marketed Magnum Bonum as 'the standard fall apple' and 'king of all fall apples,' and it was a fixture of Southern orchards from the 1830s through the 1930s. The medium, roundish fruit has thin, smooth, pale greenish-yellow skin with a light crimson blush and faint darker stripes, surrounding white, fine-grained, tender, juicy flesh that is mildly subacid and aromatic. It ripens in mid-to-late summer across most of the South and is prized as a dessert apple as well as a good keeper for its season, with a vigorous, productive, disease-tolerant tree habit that made it a dependable dooryard choice. Provide a compatible pollinizer such as Horse, Yates, or Shockley, since Magnum Bonum sets fruit best with cross-pollination.
sources: Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples

common_name: Camak's Sweet Apple (Rediscovered Carolina-Georgia Heirloom Sweet Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun; this variety was widely grown across the South from the mid-1800s until it nearly vanished in the early 1900s, and was rediscovered in 1997 when a Georgia grower brought fruit to pomologist Lee Calhoun for identification, so give it a nearby pollinizer since it is not self-fruitful.

directions: Camak's Sweet is a medium-to-large, round apple with smooth, matte-yellow skin blushed red on the sun-exposed side and marked with abundant, slightly raised tan russet lenticels. The yellowish flesh is fine-grained, firm, and juicy, with a distinctly sweet, aromatic flavor rather than the tart profile typical of most Old Southern cider and cooking apples. It is a very late-season variety and an excellent keeper, historically valued for fresh winter eating once tarter apples had been used up. Considered extinct for decades until its 1997 rediscovery, it is now maintained by a handful of Southern heirloom orchards preserving Lee Calhoun-documented cultivars.
sources: Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples (2nd ed.)

common_name: Disharoon Apple (Rediscovered Georgia Heirloom Dessert Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Disharoon originated in Habersham County, Georgia around 1855 and, once thought extinct, has since been recovered by Southern heirloom orchards, so plant a second apple cultivar nearby for reliable cross-pollination.

directions: Named for the north Georgia grower on whose land it was found in the mid-1850s, Disharoon produces medium, roundish fruit flattened at the ends, with green skin taking on a yellowish-gold hue on the sunny side and numerous obscure greenish, russet-centered dots. The pale yellow flesh is tender, moderately juicy, crisp, and sweet, making it a well-regarded dessert apple rather than primarily a cooking or cider type. Fruit ripens in September to October, fitting into the early-fall harvest window for Deep South orchards. Long believed extinct, it survives today only in a few Southern heirloom collections working from Lee Calhoun's documentation of Georgia's old apple varieties.
sources: Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples

common_name: Rusty Coat Apple (Heavily Russeted Southern Heirloom Keeper)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun; the heavy natural russeting that gives Rusty Coat its name also sheds moisture and resists cracking better than smooth-skinned Southern apples, and it needs a second cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Rusty Coat was, by the 19th century, a name applied broadly to any old Southern apple whose greenish-yellow skin was heavily overlaid with coarse, dry russet, but the strain preserved by today's heirloom orchards has become the standard bearer for the type. Fruit is small to medium with faint red striping showing through the rough russet coat, and the crisp, tender flesh is somewhat dry with a pleasant, sweet, nutty flavor rather than sharp acidity. It ripens in late September to early October and is an outstanding long keeper, historically used for drying and as a late-winter dessert apple once smoother-skinned varieties had gone soft in storage. Its thick russet coat also gives it more resistance to cracking and disease pressure than many thin-skinned Southern heirlooms, a useful trait in humid Gulf South summers.
sources: Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples

common_name: Royal Limbertwig Apple (Warm-Climate Southern Limbertwig Strain)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun and stake loosely while young, since the supple, drooping ('limber') branches typical of the family need support under a heavy crop; unlike many Limbertwig strains bred in the cooler mountains, Royal Limbertwig is noted for performing well in the warmer Deep South, though it still needs a second apple cultivar for pollination.

directions: Royal Limbertwig is one of the best-regarded of the more than one hundred Limbertwig strains documented by Lee Calhoun, singled out among heirloom nurseries as a high-quality apple that grows well in the warmer areas of the South, making it a more Gulf-Coast-friendly choice than many mountain-bred Limbertwig selections. Fruit is medium to large with yellow skin overlaid with red, and the fine-grained, juicy, tender flesh is mildly subacid with the rich, old-fashioned flavor the Limbertwig family is known for. It ripens in October and keeps well, making it useful for fresh eating, cooking, and cider alike. Like other Limbertwigs it is not self-fruitful, so plant a second apple cultivar within pollination range.
sources: Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples

common_name: Black Limbertwig Apple (Slow Food Ark of Taste Southern Cider Limbertwig)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun and stake loosely while young to support the characteristically supple, drooping branches; this strain wants a moderate 600-700 chill hours, so it is best suited to the upper Piedmont and cooler pockets of zones 6-8 rather than the hottest Gulf Coast locations, and needs a second apple cultivar for pollination.

directions: Black Limbertwig is a Slow Food USA Ark of Taste-listed heirloom, one of the darkest-skinned of the many Southern Limbertwig strains, with red fruit deepening over a green background as it ripens in October. The yellow flesh is juicy with a distinctive smoky, musky tang layered over a deep sweet base, a flavor profile Southern heirloom orchardists rate among the best of the Limbertwig family for cider and apple butter. Like its relatives it takes its name from limber, drooping twigs that bend rather than snap under a heavy crop. It is not self-fruitful and should be planted with another apple cultivar for cross-pollination.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste, Black Limbertwig Apple
Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples
Century Farm Orchards — Limbertwig Apple Descriptions

common_name: Caney Fork Limbertwig Apple (Cumberland Mountains Heirloom Keeper)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun and stake loosely while young for the supple, drooping branches typical of the Limbertwig family; originating in the Cumberland Mountains of Kentucky, it wants a higher chill accumulation of roughly 650-750 hours and performs best in the cooler upper South rather than the low-chill Gulf Coast, and needs a second apple cultivar for pollination.

directions: Caney Fork Limbertwig takes its name from the Caney Fork area of Kentucky's Cumberland Mountains, and produces medium-to-large, round, symmetrical fruit with dull yellow skin mostly covered by a bright red flush and prominent white dots. The crisp, juicy, yellowish flesh has a sweet, spicy, fruity flavor and a firm, moderately breaking texture that makes it equally good for fresh eating and for cooking. It ripens in early October and is an excellent long keeper, a trait shared with most of the Limbertwig family. As with other Limbertwig strains it is not self-fruitful and needs a compatible apple cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.
sources: Creighton Lee Calhoun, Old Southern Apples
Big Horse Creek Farm — Caney Fork Limbertwig
